A neighbouring developer is building a substation that could also connect your farm, cutting both projects' costs if the two share its design and construction.
A sprint review suggests that adding battery-health alerts would make the operator more likely to renew its monitoring contract, though not certain to.

options.text: Exploit: act to make sure the opportunity happens
options.rationale: Committing the crew removes the uncertainty: the early start happens because the project makes it happen. Exploiting suits an opportunity that one action within the project's control can secure.

options.text: Share: give part of it to a party better able to capture it
options.rationale: Neither project can capture the substation saving alone. Sharing the benefit with the developer, who controls half of it, is what makes the saving achievable for both.

options.text: Enhance: raise its likelihood or the size of its benefit
options.rationale: The alerts make renewal more likely without guaranteeing it, which is enhancement. The operator's decision stays outside the project, so the most the team can do is improve the odds.

options.text: Accept: take the benefit if it comes, without acting on it
options.rationale: Not used. Each opportunity here needs action to be captured: without a crew, a partner or the new alerts, the benefit is likely to pass. Acceptance suits opportunities where pursuing them would cost more than they are worth.

questions.explanation: Opportunity responses mirror threat responses and are chosen by how much control the project has over the outcome. Exploit when a project action can make the benefit certain, enhance when you can only improve its odds or size, share when a partner is needed to capture it, and accept when pursuing it costs more than it returns. Opportunities left in the register without a response are usually lost by default.
questions.mindset: Plan for the upside with the same care you give the downside.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is building a research vessel, with the hull fabricated to a fixed plan and the onboard science systems developed iteratively with the scientists. Complete each sentence with the approach that best addresses the uncertainty described. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Hull welding output varies from week to week between 80 and 120 metres, with no single event behind it, so the hull schedule is best protected by
Nobody can yet say how the scientists will want instruments laid out on deck, because they will only know once they try them, so this is best handled by
Earlier first-of-a-kind vessels met problems that nobody could have listed in advance, so the project should prepare for surprises of that kind by

options.text: modelling the range of outcomes and planning with buffers sized from it
options.rationale: Variability is a spread around a known quantity rather than an event that may or may not happen. Modelling the range and sizing buffers from it protects the plan without pretending any single week's output can be predicted.

options.text: delivering in increments with prototypes and trials, so understanding grows before commitments are made
options.rationale: This is ambiguity: the answer does not yet exist to be estimated. Prototypes and trials with the scientists create the knowledge, and the iterative stream is built to absorb what is learned.

options.text: building resilience through management reserve, design margins and fast decision routes
options.rationale: Emergent risks cannot be listed, so they cannot be given individual responses. Reserve, margin and the ability to decide quickly let the project absorb whatever does appear.

options.text: transferring the exposure to the shipyard through a fixed-price contract clause
options.rationale: Not used. Transfer works for risks that can be defined and priced. None of these can be, so a fixed-price clause would either be priced very high or end in dispute when the uncertainty materialises.

questions.explanation: Not all uncertainty is a discrete event with a probability and an impact. Variability, a spread around a known quantity, is managed by modelling the range and protecting with buffers; ambiguity, not yet knowing what is true or wanted, is reduced by learning through experiments and increments; emergent risk that cannot be identified in advance is met with resilience. Forcing all three into event-style register entries produces responses that change nothing.
questions.mindset: Match the response to the kind of uncertainty, not just to its size.

questions.stem: Your agile team building a payroll app tracks risk exposure as probability × impact in days, summed across open risks, and plots it each sprint. At the start of sprint 5 there are four risks: data migration (50%, 20 days), tax-table updates (30%, 10 days), single sign-on integration (40%, 15 days) and app-store review (20%, 5 days). During the sprint a spike closes the single sign-on risk and testing cuts data migration to 25%. Nothing else changes. Work out the exposure before and after the sprint.

blanks.label: Total risk exposure at the start of sprint 5, in days
blanks.rationale: 0.50 × 20 = 10, 0.30 × 10 = 3, 0.40 × 15 = 6 and 0.20 × 5 = 1, which sum to 20 days of exposure across the four open risks.

blanks.label: Total risk exposure at the end of sprint 5, in days
blanks.rationale: Single sign-on is closed and contributes nothing; data migration falls to 0.25 × 20 = 5. The other two are unchanged at 3 and 1, so the total is 5 + 3 + 1 = 9 days.

blanks.label: Reduction in exposure during the sprint, as a percentage of the starting figure
blanks.rationale: The exposure fell by 20 − 9 = 11 days, and 11 ÷ 20 = 0.55, a 55% reduction. Of that, 6 days came from closing single sign-on and 5 from halving the migration probability.

questions.explanation: A risk burndown sums the exposure of open risks each sprint, so the team and its stakeholders can see whether uncertainty is actually being retired as features are delivered. The useful reading is the trend and the work behind it: a flat or rising line means risk work is not getting into sprints, while a steep fall shows which spikes and tests are paying off. Exposure in days is only as good as the probabilities behind it, so the scores need revisiting each sprint.
questions.mindset: Measure whether risk is going down, not just whether features are going out.

questions.stem: Your refinery turnaround's risk analysis produced this sensitivity chart, with five inputs shown in register order. Each bar shows how far the finish date moves as that one input ranges from its low to its high estimate, with every other input held at its most likely value. Management will fund one further study to narrow the forecast range as much as possible. Select the input to study.

graphic.title: Sensitivity chart of five inputs against turnaround finish date, centre line at the planned finish
graphic.caption: Select a bar. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between bars, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Crane availability: finish moves from 1 day early to 4 days late; highest probability rating on the register
regions.rationale: A high probability rating says how likely the risk is, not how much it moves the forecast. Its 5-day swing is one of the smaller ones, so studying it would narrow the range little.

regions.label: Catalyst delivery: finish moves from on time to 9 days late; the largest possible delay of any input
regions.rationale: This bar reaches furthest to the late side, which is why it tempts, but its total swing is 9 days. The candidate has read the worst case instead of the width of the bar.

regions.label: Heat-exchanger repair scope: finish moves from 4 days early to 8 days late
regions.rationale: A 12-day swing, the widest on the chart. Narrowing the uncertainty in this input does most to narrow the forecast, because it contributes most to the spread.

regions.label: Contractor productivity: finish moves from 3 days early to 3 days late
regions.rationale: A symmetrical 6-day swing. The candidate may see two-sided uncertainty as the most uncertain, but its width is half that of the widest bar.

regions.label: Permit-to-work delays: finish moves from on time to 3 days late; most frequent issue on past turnarounds
regions.rationale: Frequency on past jobs is a good identification prompt, but here the input moves the finish by only 3 days. The candidate has ranked by familiarity instead of by sensitivity.

questions.explanation: A sensitivity chart ranks inputs by how much each one, varied alone, moves the outcome, and the width of a bar, from its low end to its high end, is that measure. To narrow a forecast, reduce uncertainty in the widest bar first; neither the furthest single extreme, the probability rating nor how often a problem occurred elsewhere tells you how much an input drives the spread. Read the whole width, then confirm the input can actually be studied or influenced.
questions.mindset: Spend analysis effort where the uncertainty moves the answer most.
